The results isolate creep as the primary driver of failure, predicting that combined stresses will cause tank floor failure after few years of operation. - Tank design – Tanks are usually designed following guidelines from API 650 and ASME BPVC Section II standards. However, important differences among tank designs have been observed, specifically in the salt distribution ring, piping network, and foundation, highlighting the need for a standard dedicated to molten salt TES tanks. Design features could be modified to reduce stress and deformation during operation. For instance, the sparger ring design could be improved to enhance mixing between salt inflow and inventory, and the floor thickness could be increased to reduce high stress during operation. - Tank fabrication – The tank welding fabrication process for molten salt TES tanks leads to high residual stress and distortion, which strongly influence operational stress. High residual stress could lead to stress relaxation cracking during operation, while significant distortion in the tank floor could facilitate the formation of buckles. Welding processes should focus on producing tank floors with lower residual stress and distortion. - Operation conditions – One of the most critical tank operating conditions that lead to high stress during operation occurs when a temperature difference between the salt inflow and a low inventory salt arises. This is exacerbated by high inflow mass flow rates. This operating condition is common at the tank's daily start, and the adverse effects could be minimized by making operational decisions such as maintaining a safe inventory level at the end of operation and regulating salt mass flow rates at low inventory levels. 5 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. 2 Tank Size Analysis 2.1 Geometry Generation and Model Setup The existing validated molten salt tank model was modified in the ANSYS Design Modeler environment to enable flexible tank geometry development. This allowed for modifying the diameter and floor thickness while maintaining the proportions of the sparger ring and foundation. Within the geometry tool, a first tank design was generated by considering a radial section of the tank, composed of a cylinder segment and a sub-dome roof. Three shell-type elements were used to represent the tank geometry: the floor, wall, and roof. A circular pattern operation was then implemented to obtain the final simulation geometry. Dividing the tank into pieces corresponding to different levels facilitates the generation of a structured hexahedral mesh. The geometry generation used a function in which the tank diameter is a variable that can be adjusted to represent tanks with diameters ranging from 20 m to 42 m.
